items.content:
I spent much of the weekend talking with the team who did this work. Seb--and everyone else--acted with integrity and generosity throughout.

Initially we believed the other team had also solved the problem. We wanted to collaborate and do a joint release. 

When we learned that they had Euler but not Navier-Stokes, we offered to let them go first, to suggest that they should be the ones to get the prize, and optionally for Tristan to be the lead author on a rewrite of the OpenAI proof. We felt it was challenging to offer the same to Levent (an Anthropic employee), who was not willing to talk or coordinate with us anyway. We were open to other solutions.

We would have greatly preferred coordination. We did not rush to publish even though the other team wasn't communicating with us. The team threatened us with unfounded accusations of plagarism.

Now that we can see their work, the approaches appear to be different. It is also worth noting that our latest model can solve many, many other math problems.

It is true that we tried this because there were rumors on the internet last week that Anthropic's models had solved a millennium problem and we were curious if ours could do it too.

Synthetic data derived from production user data of consumer AI tools is used for training. I’ve heard this rumour from both large labs’ employees. 

In particular, if you’re doing something “interesting” like working on complex math/business/software/bio problems you’re dramatically more likely to get trained on because they filter/up-weight towards those usecases where the model has the most to learn.

Even in ZDR and “we won’t train on you” regimes, derivative data is usually carved out. The promise is only not to train on exactly the data you put in, rewritten data is fair game.

items.content:
well obviously the data gets 'touched'.. it's being processed by the provider. then the question is do you store it or delete it once you're done processing, ZDR says you delete it.

what you choose define as "processing" a request is important, it will of course include generation of the response sent back to the user, but also a suite of other derivative actions like collection of analytics (stuff like using a model to classifying the usecase, safety screening, etc), billing data, and potentially synthetic data.

what you have to delete is the original request, derivate data you use to bill the customer, monitor use, keep product analytics, etc. are all almost always kept. It's not a huge leap to imagine that synthetic data could be considered to be derivative data.

Anyway, I have no specific knowledge beyond rumours I've heard but in a world with LLMs can observe, process, and manipulate data very very quickly, ZDR is a much weaker guarantee than you might think.

items.title: This new bill banning superintelligence could hobble the frontier AI industry (which aspires to buil...
items.content:
This new bill banning superintelligence could hobble the frontier AI industry (which aspires to build superintelligence even if it doesn’t actually know how to do so).

And the leaders of that industry have only themselves to blame.

There is a difference between superintelligence that is aligned (if such a thing is possible) and superintelligence that is not. It is at least conceivable that the former might be net positive.

So far we have neither, but a superabundance of hype combined with a striking lacking of prudence on OpenAI’s part has gotten where we are, with intense mistrust all around.

Although I don’t think this bill is formulated correctly – and risks throwing out some beneficial applications along with some bad ones – I can see why legislators have reached this point.

By not playing straight, the big tech companies have soiled their own bed.

items.title: I never look at the code when I work on ChapterPal. I didn't do that even when Claude Code didn't ex...
items.content:
I never look at the code when I work on ChapterPal. I didn't do that even when Claude Code didn't exist yet and I copied and pasted the code from the chat into the text file.

But sometimes you have to. This usually happens when your code hits the limits of the cloud service for something so simple that isn't supposed to hit any limit, so you are curious and ask the bot the question: why did it hit this particular limit (e.g., memory or CPU time)?

If you want to understand the kind of code Codex writes, here's an example that I found today when I asked that question. So the task was: I needed to create a digest of a large book to send to an LLM and ask for an executive summary. I set the maximum size of the digest to be 100,000 characters.

The approach was to take all headings, the first and the last paragraphs of each first-level section of each chapter, the full content of the introduction and conclusion chapters, and, if 100,000 characters weren't reached yet, fill the remaining space with statistically important paragraphs of each chapter in proportion to the chapter's length.

So, why would Supabase crash the execution of such a simple algorithm, saying that all CPU available to the edge function was consumed?

The answer is: Codex implemented the algorithm as follows. To decide whether to append a statistically important paragraph to the digest, it needed to know what size the digest will have after the concatenation. How did it decide to implement this? The way no good software engineer would choose:

1. Loop over all paragraphs:

2. Concatenate the current digest with the candidate paragraph.

3. Measure the length of the resulting concatenation.

4. If more characters than 100,000, pick another paragraph and repeat.

What would a non-retarded software engineer do to get the resulting length? Add A+B, where A is the length of the current digest (computed once for the entire digest) and B is the length of the paragraph (computed once for each paragraph).

So, I sad to Codex to replace the length function with a + sign and this fixed the issue.

So, if you don't read the vibe code, it's almost entirely retarded like that. And that's OK. You should just be aware of the fact and not make it responsible for running a nuclear factory.

items.content_html:
I never look at the code when I work on ChapterPal. I didn't do that even when Claude Code didn't exist yet and I copied and pasted the code from the chat into the text file.

But sometimes you have to. This usually happens when your code hits the limits of the cloud service for something so simple that isn't supposed to hit any limit, so you are curious and ask the bot the question: why did it hit this particular limit (e.g., memory or CPU time)?

If you want to understand the kind of code Codex writes, here's an example that I found today when I asked that question. So the task was: I needed to create a digest of a large book to send to an LLM and ask for an executive summary. I set the maximum size of the digest to be 100,000 characters.

The approach was to take all headings, the first and the last paragraphs of each first-level section of each chapter, the full content of the introduction and conclusion chapters, and, if 100,000 characters weren't reached yet, fill the remaining space with statistically important paragraphs of each chapter in proportion to the chapter's length.

So, why would Supabase crash the execution of such a simple algorithm, saying that all CPU available to the edge function was consumed?

The answer is: Codex implemented the algorithm as follows. To decide whether to append a statistically important paragraph to the digest, it needed to know what size the digest will have after the concatenation. How did it decide to implement this? The way no good software engineer would choose:

1. Loop over all paragraphs:

2. Concatenate the current digest with the candidate paragraph.

3. Measure the length of the resulting concatenation.

4. If more characters than 100,000, pick another paragraph and repeat.

What would a non-retarded software engineer do to get the resulting length? Add A+B, where A is the length of the current digest (computed once for the entire digest) and B is the length of the paragraph (computed once for each paragraph).

So, I sad to Codex to replace the length function with a + sign and this fixed the issue.

So, if you don't read the vibe code, it's almost entirely retarded like that. And that's OK. You should just be aware of the fact and not make it responsible for running a nuclear factory.

items.content:
We have found stable singularity on 3D Euler! 
https://t.co/40miuTjMvl

Our starting point is a physics-informed neural network (PINN) to come up with an approximate answer, and then to argue stability around that to complete the proof.

The challenge so far has been that PINNs have not been successful in discovering singularities on the current problem. A common failure mode is PINNs converging to a trivial solution. We take special care to nudge our PINN to interesting regions through a combination of constraints, and we believe this is a novel way of making PINNs work for such hard optimization problems.

We also carry out a detailed study of the transport field of our approximate profile, and show it has promising properties of local outgoing flow, essential for proving linear damping, which is an important ingredient of overall stability.

We believe that such physics-informed and physics-centric AI are critical ingredients across many areas of research involving physical systems, and  LLMs  lack such physical grounding. 

We have been working on this problem for much of this year, and we just saw the announcement by Tristan on Euler with forcing. In contrast, we consider without forcing and use a PINN formulation.  @Caltech

A new excellent textbook "Partial Differential Equations" by Victor Ivrii (2026) is now in @ChapterPal's collection.

The book provides material for learning partial differential equations through detailed coverage of wave equations, heat diffusion, and separation of variables techniques.

The textbook has many exercices in addition to those that ChapterPal can generate for the reader based on what they have read.

Here's the link: https://t.co/JHqLaM9chu
